demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, contamination appraisals are clinically atypical and hard to reconcile unless there was a specific disgust/violation element to the death exposure. The other selected appraisals ('Bad Coper' and 'Self-Comparison') fit bereavement-related PTSD more plausibly, but 'Contamination' points toward a different trauma phenomenology (e.g., assault or abuse) and is not coherent with the provided trauma type/profile.

issues.item: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one,' these two appraisals imply substantial personal responsibility for causing or entering the traumatic situation. That is hard to reconcile with an unexpected death unless there are special circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. A clinician would question whether these items fit this trauma type as stated.

vignette:
Leila had spent most of her adult life as a judge, a role that had made her accustomed to weighing facts carefully, listening for inconsistencies, and staying composed while other people unraveled. She lived in the same American city for decades with her husband, and by the time she was seventy-five, her days had settled into a disciplined rhythm of chambers, papers, and home. That order was shattered when her adult son died unexpectedly. The circumstances of his death were sudden enough that there had been no real preparation, no gradual decline to absorb, only the abrupt news that a healthy life had ended before anyone in the family could make sense of it. Leila could still recall the moment she heard, the flatness of the phone call, and how quickly the ordinary room around her seemed to lose its shape.

In the weeks that followed, she found herself returning again and again to the details of the day and to what she believed she had done wrong. She had come to believe that the event happened because of the way she acted, and that if she had handled things differently, her son might still be alive. At times she would replay ordinary conversations with him, searching for some overlooked warning, some different choice she should have made. What troubled her most was the conviction that she should have protected others and failed. As a mother, she had always seen herself as the one who could anticipate harm, ask the right questions, and keep her family steady. After his death, that sense of herself collapsed into a harsher judgment: she had not protected him, and she had not protected the people who loved him from the shock of losing him. She spoke about this with the same exacting seriousness she brought to her courtroom work, except now the verdict was turned against herself.

Leila had not only grieved; she had also become sharply aware of how she appeared to others since the death. In private, she told her husband that her reactions showed that she was a lousy coper, and she seemed embarrassed by her own tears, delays, and moments of being unable to continue with a task. This was especially painful because she had always prided herself on control. At work, she tried to keep appearing as she always had, but she found that certain moments in the courtroom or in chambers suddenly felt too exposing, and she would need to steady herself before she could continue. She did not describe herself as collapsing, but as not managing well enough, not handling it in the way she thought she should. That judgment toward herself sat alongside her ongoing grief and made it hard for her to feel proud of having kept going at all.

Over time, the death also changed the texture of her daily life in ways that were hard to hide. In the courthouse, she could still do the work, but there were moments when the contrast between the responsibilities of judging and the helplessness she felt about her son's death became overwhelming. A colleague's mention of a family holiday, a younger attorney talking about his children, or an ordinary domestic detail overheard in passing could bring the memory back with unexpected force. At home, she found herself withdrawn and preoccupied, spending long stretches sitting with the same thoughts about what she should have done. Her husband saw that she was not herself, and although he tried to reassure her, she remained fixed on the idea that she had failed in a duty that mattered more than any professional role she had ever held.

By the time she sought help, months had passed, and Leila was exhausted by the burden of living with those judgments about herself. She had reached a point where the death no longer felt like only an unbearable loss; it had become, in her mind, evidence against her own character as a mother and as a person who should have known how to act. What finally brought her to treatment was the recognition that she could no longer carry the story she had built around it without support. She wanted to understand how to live with the loss without feeling condemned by it, and she was most afraid that if she did not get help, she would spend the rest of her life believing she had failed the person she loved most.
